fetched_contents.text: Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotes: The weak-link model Abstract The significance of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in eukaryotic evolution remains controversial. Although many eukaryotic genes are of bacterial origin, they are often interpreted as being derived from mitochondria or plastids. Because of their fixed gene pool and gene loss, however, mitochondria and plastids alone cannot adequately explain the presence of all, or even the majority, of bacterial genes in eukaryotes. Available data indicate that no insurmountable barrier to HGT exists, even in complex multicellular eukaryotes. In addition, the discovery of both recent and ancient HGT events in all major eukaryotic groups suggests that HGT has been a regular occurrence throughout the history of eukaryotic evolution. A model of HGT is proposed that suggests both unicellular and early developmental stages as likely entry points for foreign genes into multicellular eukaryotes. Keywords: endosymbiosis, eukaryotic evolution, gene acquisition, genome evolution, organellar gene transfer Introduction About a decade ago, Doolittle et al. raised a question about the number of bacterial genes in protists, speculating that many bacterial genes should have accumulated in genomes of protists through feeding activities 1,2. Back then, horizontal gene transfer (HGT) had been documented widely as a mechanism to gain foreign genetic materials in prokaryotes, but remained largely an exotic concept in eukaryotes, with little substantial evidence. It is now clear that HGT has occurred in all major eukaryotic lineages. Horizontally acquired genes are not only frequent in unicellular eukaryotes 3–5, but also found in various multicellular eukaryotes, including cnidarians 6,7, mites 8, insects 9–12, nematodes 13–15, fish 16, and land plants 17–22. Although reports of HGT in eukaryotes are still frequently met with skepticism, evidence for HGT throughout eukaryotic evolution is abundant and increasing. In this paper, I discuss issues related to HGT in eukaryotes. Because most foreign genes reported in eukaryotes thus far are from bacteria, I will focus on bacterial genes. I argue that many bacterial genes in eukaryotes cannot be explained simply as gene transfers from mitochondria or plastids; rather, HGT in eukaryotes should be widespread and expected. Further, I propose a mechanism for integration of foreign DNA into eukaryotic genomes during unicellular or early developmental stages, when their nuclear DNA is relatively exposed to potential sources of HGT. No barrier to HGT in eukaryotes is insurmountable To understand the scale of HGT in eukaryotes, it is important to consider the presumed barriers to gene acquisition. Historically, protists were thought to be more likely to acquire genes than multicellular eukaryotes 1,3. Many protists are intimately associated with bacteria or microbial eukaryotes, which serve as food sources, pathogens, or symbionts. Certain species (e.g. Acanthamoeba sp.) can harbor a wide range of bacterial endosymbionts; in effect, they are training camps for bacterial adaptation to the intracellular environments of eukaryotic hosts 23,24. Although mitochondria and plastids – derived from α-proteobacterial and cyanobacterial endosymbionts, respectively – often receive the most prominent recognition, their bacterial ancestors likely represented only a portion of microbial diversity present within their ancient host cells. Temporal, transient, or obligate endosymbionts occur in many organisms 25, and differences between obligate endosymbionts and organelles can be marginal. For example, there has been heated debate over whether Prochlorococcus-related cyanobacterial endosymbionts (chromatophores) in Paulinella should be considered organelles 26–28. Although not to the same extent as in mitochondria and plastids, chromatophore genomes are highly reduced 29, with some essential genes transferred to the nucleus 30. Translocation machinery also has evolved to re-import the protein products of transferred genes back into chromatophores 31,32. Relative to protists, HGT is often assumed to be rare in complex multicellular eukaryotes because the physical isolation of germ cells from somatic cells may prevent foreign genes from being transmitted to offspring 33,34. Despite this assumption, recent HGT events have been frequently reported in both animals and plants 8,11,19–21,35,36. Some of these horizontally acquired genes in animals and plants are derived from symbionts, either inside or outside germ cells 7,10,36, whereas others are from free-living organisms 16. The magnitude of HGT from obligate bacterial endosymbionts to their insect hosts can be staggering 10. In some other cases, genes even were acquired from other sources to help maintain obligate endosymbionts 37. HGT appears to be particularly frequent in plant mitochondria 38–40, which often harbor mitochondrial genes from distantly related plants. It has been speculated that the acquisition of foreign genes in plant mitochondria was mediated through parasitism, transfer agents (e.g. insects, pathogens, or viruses), illegitimate pollination or other mechanisms 38,41. In any case, these foreign genes must ultimately pass through germ cells to be transmitted to the mitochondria of offspring. These data suggest that, although isolated germ cells may indeed be barriers to HGT in animals and plants, they are not insurmountable. Bacterial genes in eukaryotes: How many are of organellar origin? Given that barriers to HGT clearly are not insurmountable, we can examine available data to contemplate the number of HGT-derived genes in eukaryotes. It is well known that eukaryotic genomes contain many bacterial genes 42. Because of the α-proteobacterial and cyanobacterial origins of mitochondria and plastids, respectively, these genes are often presumed to predominantly be mitochondrial or plastid derivations 43–45. Electronic address: panaud@univ-perp.fr. * PMID: 27234293 * DOI: 10.1016/j.crvi.2016.04.013 Abstract Transposable elements (TEs) are the major components of eukaryotic genomes. A mini-report on the rarity and possible evolutionary constraints of HGT in eukaryotes

Biological and genetic reasons HGT is less common in plants and animals
The evidence points to several biological and genetic constraints that make HGT rare in eukaryotes. First, the physical separation of germ-line cells from somatic cells is often cited as a major barrier, because somatic cells may shield the germline from foreign DNA and thus reduce the chance of HGT being transmitted to offspring [N1-F1]. Second, transposable elements (TEs) themselves are major genomic components, but their transposition is tightly controlled by transcriptional and post-transcriptional pathways, which makes horizontal transfer of TEs particularly difficult [N2-F3]. Third, horizontal transfers of transposable elements are described as “long been considered as rare phenomena,” even though they appear to be more frequent in ecosystems than previously thought [N2-R1]. These factors collectively suggest that eukaryotic genomes are structured in ways that make foreign DNA acquisition less likely than in microbes, especially in complex multicellular organisms [N1-F1].

How selection pressure and genome architecture might suppress or stabilize HGT
The evidence implies that selection pressure can both suppress and stabilize HGT. If a transferred gene has no useful function, HGT is detrimental, and such genes are likely purged from the genome [N3-R1]. Conversely, when transferred genes confer a useful function—such as antibiotic resistance, parasitism, or adaptation to environmental conditions—they can be advantageous and retained [N3-R2][N3-R3]. This creates a selective landscape in which only genes that provide clear adaptive value are likely to persist. Genome architecture also matters: TEs must encode proteins essential for successful transposition, especially when those proteins are absent in the recipient genome, suggesting that genome structure imposes functional constraints on what can be horizontally acquired [N4-R2]. Additionally, the evidence notes that HGT is especially rare in eukaryotes because of technological and biological reasons, including sequencing bias and the physical isolation of germ cells [N1-F2]. This means that even when HGT does occur, it may be underrepresented in the literature unless the recipient organisms are sequenced and analyzed.

Whether the rarity implies that only rare, highly beneficial transfers are retained
The evidence supports this interpretation. The compendium of eukaryotic HGT data notes that HGT is rare in eukaryotes and that the scarcity of verified HGTs could be due to technological or biological reasons [N1-F2]. It also emphasizes that transferred genes can provide adaptive functions potentially aiding the recipient, which implies that only transfers with clear selective advantage are likely to be retained [N1-F2]. The weak-link model similarly argues that many bacterial genes in eukaryotes cannot be explained simply by mitochondria or plastid origin, but that HGT should be widespread and expected, suggesting that the rarity of verified cases reflects detection limits rather than an absence of biological reality [N1-F1]. In other words, the rarity of documented HGT events does not necessarily mean that HGT is biologically implausible; instead, it may mean that only highly beneficial transfers are retained, and that many cases remain undetected because of methodological limitations [N1-F2][N3-R1].

A mini-report on detection methods and current research limits

Which analytical techniques are used to identify HGT in eukaryotes
The evidence shows that HGT detection in eukaryotes relies on a combination of phylogenetic and sequence-based approaches. One method is HGTphyloDetect, which combines high-throughput analysis with phylogenetic inference and is designed to identify HGT events in both evolutionarily distant and closely related species [N5-F4]. It uses BLASTP hits to query a gene of interest and then calculates Alien Index (AI) scores based on the best BLAST hit in ingroup and outgroup lineages [N5-F4]. Another approach is phyletic distribution-based tools like HGT-Finder, which calculates a horizontal transfer index and probability value for each query gene [N5-F4]. AvP is also mentioned as a phylogenetic framework approach, though its phylogenetic trees are not of high quality and uncertainty remains about detecting closely related species [N5-F4]. The compendium of eukaryotic HGT data further notes that the field is increasingly using machine learning and statistical methods, but development has been slowed by a lack of validated HGTs [N1-F2]. Overall, the methods range from BLAST-based hit distribution statistics to phylogenetic reconstruction and machine learning, with a growing emphasis on high-throughput and user-friendly tools [N5-F4][N5-R5].

Limitations of phylogenetic and orthology-based inference
The evidence highlights several limitations of these methods. One is that phylogenetic trees produced by some approaches, such as AvP, may not be of high quality, and it is uncertain whether HGT events from closely related species can be detected reliably [N5-F4]. Another limitation is that orthology-based inference can be insufficient when the evolutionary history of a horizontally transferred gene disagrees with the corresponding species phylogeny [N5-R4]. The compendium also notes that simulations used to develop HGT methods often approximate very recent HGTs, but over time these sequences will be subject to mutation and selection, changing the foreign origin signal that identification methods rely on [N1-F2]. This means that inferred HGT events may be artifacts or difficult to distinguish from true events when the transferred material has been mutated or selected over time. Additionally, the evidence indicates that current HGT detection approaches are not widely suitable to the entire HGT community, and high-performance computational tools that are robust and user-friendly are urgently needed [N5-F4].

How new data or technology might change the field
New data and technology could significantly expand the field. The compendium notes that biology is experiencing an unprecedented increase in the amount of data being generated, and that the cost of sequencing genomes has decreased over the last two decades, enabling more laboratories to generate rich genomic datasets [N1-F2]. This should help identify more HGT candidates across diverse organisms. It also states that advances in machine learning and statistical methods could form the foundation for rigorous bioinformatic identification of HGTs [N1-F2]. Similarly, the evidence on HGTphyloDetect emphasizes that genome-wide identification has become increasingly practical with rapid growth in genomic data, and that high-throughput algorithms can detect HGT events from both evolutionarily distant and closely related species [N5-F4]. Taken together, these developments suggest that more data and better computational tools could reduce the current bottleneck of sparse empirical validation and help identify a broader set of HGT events with greater confidence [N1-F2][N5-F4].

Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is the non-sexual movement of genetic material between genomes, a process long recognized as pervasive in prokaryotes but less well established in eukaryotes [N3-R4]. This rarity is especially interesting because it suggests that eukaryotes have mechanisms that make HGT difficult, but also that only very useful transfers are retained when it does happen.
